blocks.text: Every developer has seen a folder like this: report_final.docx, report_final_v2.docx, report_final_v2_REAL.docx, project_backup_friday.zip. That folder is a homemade version control system. It breaks the moment two people edit the same file, the moment you need to know why a line changed, or the moment you have to rebuild exactly what ran in production three weeks ago.

items: Lost work: someone overwrites a colleague's changes while copying files around.
No history: you can see what the code is now, but not how or why it got there.
No safe experimentation: trying a risky refactor means duplicating the whole project.
No accountability: nobody can tell who introduced a bug or which change broke a feature.
No reproducibility: you cannot reliably rebuild the exact version a customer is running.

blocks.text: What a Version Control System Gives You

rows: Every saved state (commit) is kept forever, with author, timestamp and message.
You can see exactly which lines changed between any two versions, and who last touched each line.
You can develop features, fixes and experiments in parallel, isolated lines of work.
Parallel work can be combined, with the tool detecting and reporting overlapping edits.
Many people can work on one codebase and exchange changes in a controlled way.
Any past release can be checked out exactly; history doubles as an audit trail.
CI/CD systems react to new commits, which is the foundation for the second half of this course.

blocks.text: Older systems such as Subversion (SVN) and Perforce are centralized: one server holds the history, and developers check out a working copy. Git is distributed: every clone is a complete repository with the full history, so most operations (commit, log, diff, branch, merge) are local and fast, and there is no single point of failure.

rows: Requires network access to the server
Local; sharing is a separate step (push)
Cheap: a branch is a 41-byte pointer file
Needs extensions such as Git LFS

blocks.text: Conceptually, Git stores snapshots. Each commit records the complete state of the project tree at that moment. Unchanged files are not duplicated; the new snapshot simply points to the same stored content as before. This differs from older systems that modelled history as a chain of per-file deltas. You will see exactly how this works in the chapter on Git internals.

Interview nuance: "Git stores snapshots" describes the data model. On disk, Git compresses objects into packfiles, and packfiles do use delta compression between similar objects. The model is snapshots; the storage optimization uses deltas. Being able to state both precisely signals real understanding.

Git is the version control tool: open-source software that runs on your machine. GitHub (like GitLab, Bitbucket or Azure DevOps) is a hosting platform built around Git repositories. It adds collaboration features Git itself does not have: Pull Requests, code review, issues, access control, branch protection and GitHub Actions for CI/CD. You can use Git with no hosting platform at all; you cannot use GitHub's repository features without Git.
When someone says "push it to Git", they almost always mean "push it to the remote repository on GitHub". In interviews, keep the two terms distinct.
